title: The SIR exercise is also a technology failure
shows: Priya Seetharaman, a professor in the Management Information Systems Group at the Indian Institute of Management Calcutta, reads the revision as a digital project run through the Commission's ERONet platform, and finds it fails tests that a large system rollout is expected to pass. She writes that notices for logical discrepancy were raised centrally by filters such as the gap in age between parent and child and the number of children linked to one parent, although ages on Indian rolls are often approximate, and that a rule coded into the platform, never published by the Commission, decides who must appear for a hearing. She says matching an elector to a parent on the 2002 roll compares family names across decades and scripts without having been tested at scale, citing West Bengal's 2002 rolls, which were in Bengali and were rendered into English with machine tools, over 1.3 crore entries flagged there, and counsel's statement to the Supreme Court that more than half the logical discrepancy cases were variations in names. She writes that features changed while the revision was under way, among them de-duplication software the Commission had told the Supreme Court in late 2025 could not be relied on and later switched back on in some States, and a mapping check that made booth level officers redo finished work. She says new ERONet options in October letting registration officers dispose of notice cases without hearings were explained through demonstration videos, video conferences and WhatsApp groups, so that the software stood in for the written rule, and that the online Form 6 carried a declaration on parents and grandparents that is not in the statutory form. She ends on the timetable, noting that enumeration in Tamil Nadu and West Bengal ran about six weeks with final rolls in February for polls in April, and that West Bengal's final roll was published with over half a crore names still under adjudication.
quote: The 2025-26 SIR is the first revision of this scale to be run through a centralised digital platform, and the technology itself has become a source of exclusion.
Additionally, a rule coded into the software platform decides who must appear for a hearing. This rule has never been published by the Commission
note: First reading, 13 November 2026, from the page of the Chennai print edition of 13 November that the owner sent, read in full. The online article at this address is behind The Hindu's subscription wall and shows only the opening paragraphs, which agree with the print text, and its standfirst repeats the print pull quote. The byline gives the author as Professor, Management Information Systems Group, Indian Institute of Management Calcutta. The figures and claims are the author's as she states them, and the 1.3 crore and the counsel's statement are given as she reports them. Her verdicts that the revision is a failure of digital governance and her closing view on whether the failures were foreseen are her own and are not carried.
